newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says Iraq to blame for food delays.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says Iraq to blame for food delays.

text.p: The United States accused Iraq on Monday of being "farcical" in complaining about the slow delivery of U.N.-sanctioned humanitarian goods under an "oil-for-food" deal and said Baghdad itself was to blame.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns acknowledged delays in the U.N.-approved "oil-for-food" deal that went into effect in December.

But he said the main reason for the delays is that "the Iraqis are dragging their feet ... delaying access to transportation and communications by the U.N. monitors and are denying the U.N. monitors the full freedom of movement the U.N. was promised."
"This is getting to be farcical ... If anyone is to blame for U.N. resolution 986's slowness it is the Iraqi government themselves," Burns said.

As part of the deal that allowed the U.N. Security Council to approve the resolution, Iraq signed a painstakingly negotiated memorandum of understanding with the United Nations that details the kind of support Baghdad must allow the U.N. monitors and "these conditionsm are not being met," Burns said.
Iraq's U.N. envoy complained on Monday to Secretary-General Kofi Annan over delays in the arrival of humanitarian goods under the "oil-for-food" deal.

"We are today more than two months from ... the start (of the deal) and no kilo (2.2 pounds) of rice or sugar or whatever has really arrived in Iraq," ambassador Nizar Hamdoon told reporters after a meeting with the U.N. chief.
"They are expecting something to arrive in March. I only reflected on the frustration that we are having in Iraq on this operation," he added.

Under the "oil-for-food" agreement between Iraq and the United Nations, which entered into force on Dec. 10, Baghdad is allowed to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy humanitarian items to mitigate the effects of sanctions in force since Iraq's August 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

Hamdoon said some contracts for food and other items had been approved by the U.N. sanctions committee, "but nothing has arrived in the country up till this minute." He faulted what he said were delays within the U.N. sanctions committee, which must approve contracts for Iraqi purchases.
